_about: The only place performance budget numbers live (docs/RELEASE_STANDARD.md, section 2). tools/perf_check.py compares its medians, and the store step's figures, with 'budgets' and exits 1 when a figure is over. After each improvement, lower a budget to the new figure plus 15%. Raise one only with a stated reason in the pull request.
machine: No named reference machine (owner decision, 18 Oct 2026, #121). These budgets were set on the development laptop (baseline.machine) and apply to whichever Windows machine measures: each release is measured on the machine that prepares it, which tools/perf_check.py records in the report ('machine') and the release notes state (tools/evidence.py machine). The recommended 8 cores and 16 GB is a design aim, not a gate. The idle, start-up and memory budgets stay provisional, having come from one quick run, until a release run's medians lower them; the drafts-off recording budgets came from a release run, the drafts-on ones from the owner (_budget_notes), and the store and workspace_s budgets from v0.5.0-preview.4's release run (_budget_notes). A slower machine may fail one; raising a budget still needs a stated reason in the pull request.

baseline.tool: tools/perf_check.py --quick (1 run, 20 s settle, 60 s windows). startup_s is imports plus window creation until the meeting list has rendered; interpreter start and opening the workspace are not included. Since #339 (after this baseline) the window's backend, which the app loads alongside its imports, is also counted, with the imports.
baseline.machine: Intel Core Ultra 7 255H, 16 logical processors, 31.4 GB, Windows 11 (10.0.26200), WebView2 155.0.4283.45, mains power. Deviations from section 2: Performance power plan rather than Balanced, and other apps and WebView2 windows running.

targets._about: Where the ratchet is heading (#124). CPU and start-up targets are proposals to confirm from release runs. Private-bytes targets are not set yet. The #124 proposal (350 MB visible, 250 MB minimised) came before any private-bytes measurement; the first baseline is about 760 MB across 8 processes, most of it WebView2, so the targets wait for a release run's medians.

_budget_notes.minimised: Not lowered by R8 (#129), on purpose. Single quick runs on this busy development laptop on 16 Oct 2026 put minimised CPU within noise of main (R8 0.208 and 0.338% of one core; main 0.365 and 0.547%), so ratcheting on them would cause false failures. The repeatable gain was working memory: a private working set of about 70 MB minimised against about 203 MB on main. Private bytes did not change (about 755 MB), because suspending trims working memory, not commit. What CPU remains when minimised is likely mostly the Python side's one-second loops (R7, #128); perf_check reports only the whole tree, so this is not yet measured. Re-ratchet from a release run's median of three runs.
_budget_notes.worker: A fixed criterion, not a ratchet: the worker's idle unload time (120 s, workspace/worker.py) plus 5 s.
_budget_notes.leak: A fixed criterion from #124: at most 10 MB growth over 30 minutes idle (run with --leak-minutes 30). Not yet measured.
_budget_notes.recording-drafts: The owner's decision of 25 Oct 2026 (#104, #189 sitting 8): recording with live drafts on has its own budgets, 40% of one core with the window visible and about 10% minimised; drafts keep running while minimised. #216's 25% and 1% stay for recording with drafts off. Set by the owner, not raised from a quick run (E2). The evidence was a 13-minute real-sound run on PR #336's commit 4bf22fb, measured with 5-second samples of the whole process tree, a stand-in for perf_check: 35.0% visible (Python 12.7%, WebView2 22.4%) and 8.8% minimised. Intervals where a process started or ended were dropped, and the window may have been partly behind the browser. They waited in 'pending_budgets' until tools/perf_check.py gained the drafts-on states (#104 slice 4), which record public speech (--speech, such as the AMI meeting ES2004a, CC BY 4.0) with Parakeet v2 copied from --draft-models, because synthetic noise does not exercise the speech model. Not yet measured by perf_check: re-check them against the next release run's medians.
_budget_notes.recording: The owner's decision of 23 Oct 2026 (#216): 25% of one core for recording with the window visible and 1% for recording minimised, from a release-mode run that day (tools/perf_check.py --runs 3, the meter at about 60 frames a second, a 60 Hz display kept on, on mains, Performance plan): medians 22.6 (runs 29.8, 21.5, 22.6) and 0.65 (runs 0.84, 0.65, 0.62). Unlike the idle budgets, these came from a release run, not a quick one. The visible budget stays above #124's 5% target, by the owner's choice of the meter's full-quality look at about 60 frames a second over a lower figure (#216); recording minimised is already under its 2% target. Private bytes while recording have no budget yet. perf_check measures these states with synthetic audio fed at real-time pace in place of the microphone. Where managed policy turns microphone recording off, these states are reported as not measured (policy), which fails the run now that they have budgets.
_budget_notes.import: Not set yet (null: perf_check measures and proposes it, and compares nothing). The owner's decision of 28 Oct 2026 (#376): echo cancellation may add up to about 30 s to the import of a 1-hour two-track recording (an estimate at design time, DEC-077); measured at about 50 s on a development laptop, which the owner accepted as it is on 28 Oct 2026 (DEC-078), with no speed-up follow-up required. This budget is set from a release run's figure (tools/perf_check.py's import step, once per release run, and its proposed budget), never from a development-laptop run. The step imports a synthetic 1-hour recording with both tracks at 48 kHz and the computer audio's echo on the microphone, through the app's own import (the one mix with echo cancellation, the sandboxed decoder, the store).
_budget_notes.store: Set from the first Phase C release run's medians plus 20%, never from a development-laptop run (owner decision, 21 Oct 2026, #111; set in #430). Source: evidence-perf.json attached to the v0.5.0-preview.4 release (tools/perf_check.py release mode, 3 runs, 60 s settle, 300 s windows, leak check 30 minutes; package commit 16b4e90; the report is dated 27 Oct 2026). Its figures: startup workspace_s median 0.058 s (runs 0.055, 0.060, 0.058); the store step, measured once per release run with no window: open_0_meetings_s 0.0058, open_500_meetings_s 0.0102 (median of 10 opens each), listing_500_meetings_s 0.0194, page_5000_passages_s 0.0061, search_5000_passages_s 0.0216 (median of 5 each), database_5000_passages_mb 0.99. Each budget is tools/perf_check.py's propose() of those figures (tests/test_perf_check.py holds them equal): plus 20%, rounded up to 0.01, and never closer than 0.05 to the figure, so the millisecond timings get about 0.05 s of headroom rather than a fraction of a millisecond that a slower machine would fail on noise. workspace_s bounds creating a new workspace (its database schema and its root key, protected by Windows Data Protection, CryptProtectData), not unlocking an existing key, which open_0_meetings_s bounds. The store step is measured once per release run, not per run, so its figures are compared as measured; --quick has no store step and does not compare them. tools/evidence.py requires the store figures in a release's performance evidence. The 5,000-passage test in tests/test_app.py keeps its 2.0 s limit.
